title: Photographer
oneLiner: Generated images killed the stock market. They cannot attend your wedding.
summary: Photography splits cleanly along one line: whether the image has to be of something that really happened. Everything on the imaginary side — stock, catalogue product shots, concept imagery, generic lifestyle — has collapsed, because a client can now describe the picture instead of commissioning it. Everything on the real side holds, and holds firmly. A wedding happened once. A newborn is this size for two weeks. A press photograph is worthless if it was generated. Editing and retouching hours are also disappearing, which quietly removes the post-production income that carried many photographers between shoots.

tasks.name: Stock & concept imagery
tasks.note: Generated on demand, licence-free, in any style. This market did not shrink; it evaporated.

tasks.name: Standard product photography
tasks.note: AI generates or heavily augments packshots from a single reference. Premium and tactile products still get shot.

tasks.name: Retouching & culling
tasks.note: Automated selection, masking, skin work and sky replacement. A substantial post-production income line, gone.

tasks.name: Basic editorial illustration
tasks.note: Publications generate accompanying imagery rather than licensing it — except where the image must document something real.

tasks.name: Weddings, ceremonies and live events
tasks.note: It happened once, you had to be there, and the client is buying a person they trust in the room on the most important day of their year.

tasks.name: Photojournalism & documentary
tasks.note: The entire value is the claim 'this really happened'. Generated imagery makes an accountable human witness more valuable, not less.

tasks.name: Portraiture with real people
tasks.note: Getting a real person to relax and look like themselves is interpersonal work performed in a room.

tasks.name: Directing a real shoot
tasks.note: Light, location, crew, weather and a client changing their mind at 9am. Logistics and taste under live conditions.

whatSurvives: Images of things that actually happened, taken by someone the client trusted to be there.
adaptPrompt:
You are my photography business assistant. You handle the words and the planning around the work; the shooting is mine.

For client work:
1. Turn a client conversation into a shot list: must-haves, nice-to-haves, and the shots they will be upset about later if nobody mentioned them.
2. Build a run of show with timings, light conditions by hour for the date and location, and the fallback plan for weather.
3. Draft the client-facing questionnaire that surfaces what they actually want — including the family and relationship details that go wrong at events if you do not ask in advance.

For the business, which is where I actually lose money:
4. Draft contracts and terms for review: deliverables, timeline, usage rights, cancellation, weather clause. Flag anything I should have a lawyer look at.
5. Write the follow-up sequence: enquiry reply, booking confirmation, pre-shoot prep, gallery delivery, review request.
6. Price analysis: given my costs, hours including editing, and target income, tell me what my day rate has to be and where my current pricing is losing money.

Rules: never write copy claiming I shot something I did not, and never suggest passing generated images off as photographs — that risk is existential in this business. When you draft client communication, keep it warm and short; nobody reads a five-paragraph email about their own wedding.
